writing.prompt:
Part I Writing (30 minutes)

Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay on the importance of trust in relationships. You can base your essay on the following three relationships: between employers and employees, between businesses and customers, or between teachers and students. You can cite examples to illustrate your point. You should write at least 150 words but no more than 200 words.
writing.ideas: 审题思路:本题为现象分析类,要求论述「信任」在某一类关系中的重要性。推荐三段式:① 首段点明信任是一切合作关系的地基,选定一组关系(建议选师生关系或企业-客户,素材最多);② 中间段用正反对比论证:有信任则成本低、效率高,无信任则防御重重、合作瓦解,可举具体场景;③ 结尾回扣主题并给出建立信任的可操作做法。注意不要三个关系都写,只选一组深入写。
writing.model:
Among the many forces that hold a relationship together, trust is the quietest yet the most powerful. Whether between employers and employees, businesses and customers, or teachers and students, trust determines how far a relationship can go.
Take the relationship between teachers and students as an example. A class built on trust looks relaxed but disciplined: students dare to ask naive questions, admit what they do not understand, and accept criticism as help rather than attack. The teacher, in return, spends less energy on suspicion and control and more on actual teaching. By contrast, once trust breaks down, even a reasonable requirement sounds like a trap, and every conversation turns into negotiation. The cost of distrust is not only emotional; it shows up in wasted time, defensive behaviour and missed opportunities to learn.
Fortunately, trust can be built deliberately. It grows from consistency—doing what was promised, again and again—and from honesty about mistakes. Those who keep their word in small things earn the right to be believed in big ones.
writing.notes: 亮点:① 首句 quietest yet the most powerful 对比修辞,直接切题;② 中间段采用正反对比(relaxed but disciplined vs. breaks down),场景具体;③ 结尾给出可操作建议(consistency / honesty),避免空喊口号。加分表达:hold a relationship together, the cost of distrust, earn the right to be believed。

listening.intro:
Questions 1 to 4 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

【听力原文】
M: Hey Lisa, you look exhausted. Another late shift at the café?
W: Yeah, four evenings a week. My mum keeps saying I should quit and focus on my studies.
M: I get her point, but honestly the job has taught me more than I expected. Last week I handled a customer who was furious about a wrong order, and I stayed calm until he apologized to me.
W: That is exactly the kind of thing résumés cannot show. Transferable skills—patience, communication, handling pressure—employers value them highly.
M: My plan is to keep the job through this semester, then cut back to weekends before graduation.
W: Reasonable. Just make sure your grades do not slip; that is the line you cannot cross.
listening.questions:
1. Why does the woman look exhausted?
A) She stayed up late preparing for exams.
B) She has been working evening shifts.
C) She argued with her mother.
D) She attended a late-night lecture.

2. What did the woman do last week?
A) She calmed down an angry customer.
B) She corrected a wrong order.
C) She quit her job at the café.
D) She apologized to a customer.

3. What does the man say the job has taught him?
A) How to write a better résumé.
B) How to manage his budget.
C) Skills that cannot be shown on a résumé.
D) The importance of good grades.

4. What is the woman's plan for the future?
A) To quit immediately.
B) To work four evenings a week forever.
C) To find an office job after graduation.
D) To reduce working hours before graduation.
listening.analysis:
1. B。开头男士问 Another late shift at the café,女士回答 Yeah, four evenings a week,说明疲惫原因是晚间打工。
2. A。女士提到上周处理了一位因订单出错而大怒的顾客,并保持冷静直到对方向她道歉。B 是背景信息非她所为;D 主客颠倒。
3. C。男士说 Transferable skills... employers value them highly,即工作教会了他简历上看不到的能力。
4. D。女士计划本学期继续,毕业前减到周末,对应 reduce working hours before graduation。

listening.intro:
Questions 5 to 7 are based on the passage you have just heard.

【听力原文】
Students often boast about pulling an all-nighter before an exam, but sleep researchers say the practice is closer to studying with one hand tied behind your back. During deep sleep, the brain replays the day experiences and moves new memories from temporary storage to long-term storage. Cut sleep short, and this transfer is interrupted—exactly the material you need at nine the next morning.
In one experiment, students who slept eight hours after studying recalled forty percent more vocabulary than students who stayed awake, even though the awake group spent those extra hours reviewing. The reviewing group felt more confident, but confidence was not accuracy.
Researchers suggest a simple rule: study, then sleep, then test. A twenty-minute nap after an afternoon study session can restore memory performance to morning levels. So the next time you consider sacrificing sleep for one more chapter, remember: sleep is not the reward for studying; it is part of the studying.
listening.questions:
5. What does the brain do during deep sleep?
A) It invents new dreams.
B) It moves memories to long-term storage.
C) It stops all brain activity.
D) It reviews vocabulary aloud.

6. How much more vocabulary did the sleeping group recall?
A) Twenty percent.
B) Thirty percent.
C) Forty percent.
D) Sixty percent.

7. What rule do researchers suggest?
A) Study, sleep, then test.
B) Test, study, then sleep.
C) Sleep, test, then study.
D) Review all night, then sleep.
listening.analysis:
5. B。深睡阶段大脑回放白天经历,把新记忆从临时存储转入长期存储。
6. C。实验中睡足八小时的学生多回忆起百分之四十的词汇。
7. A。研究者建议的简单规则是 study, then sleep, then test。

listening.intro:
Questions 8 to 10 are based on the lecture you have just heard.

【听力原文】
Good morning. Today we will discuss a trend that is quietly changing the skyline of dense cities: vertical greenery. As urban land becomes scarce, architects have begun to move gardens upward—onto walls, balconies and rooftops.
The benefits are measurable. A wall covered in climbing plants can lower the surface temperature of a building by up to ten degrees on a summer afternoon, reducing air-conditioning bills significantly. Green roofs absorb rainwater, easing the burden on drainage systems during storms, and they filter airborne dust, which matters greatly in polluted cities. Singapore offers a famous example: since 2009, new buildings above a certain size have been required to replace every square metre of green land they occupy with equivalent planting on the structure itself.
However, the approach is not without challenges. Irrigation, structural load and maintenance costs must be planned from the start, and poorly designed installations can damage buildings rather than protect them. Critics also point out that vertical greenery is no substitute for parks at street level; it complements them, not replaces them. As with most urban innovations, the lesson is balance: technology and nature can share a wall, if the wall is designed for both.
listening.questions:
8. What can a wall of climbing plants do on a summer afternoon?
A) Lower the building surface temperature.
B) Increase air-conditioning bills.
C) Absorb all rainwater.
D) Block sunlight completely.

9. What has Singapore required since 2009?
A) All buildings must have rooftops.
B) New large buildings must replace green land with planting on the structure.
C) Parks must be built downtown.
D) Gardens must be watered daily.

10. What is the lecturer's final point about vertical greenery?
A) It replaces street-level parks.
B) It is too expensive to be useful.
C) It complements rather than replaces parks.
D) It should be banned in dense cities.
listening.analysis:
8. A。覆盖攀缘植物的墙面夏季午后可降低建筑表面温度至多十度。
9. B。新加坡自 2009 年起要求一定规模以上的新建筑在建筑本体上补植等面积绿化。
10. C。讲座结尾:垂直绿化不能取代地面公园,而是补充(complements them, not replaces them)。

reading.title: The Hidden Cost of Always Being Reachable
reading.passage:
The average office worker now checks email more than seventy times a day and answers a message every six minutes. Each interruption looks harmless—a few seconds, a quick reply—but researchers who study attention have found that the real cost is not the interruption itself; it is the time the brain needs to rebuild the original train of thought afterwards. In experiments, participants who were interrupted during a writing task took, on average, twice as long to finish and reported far more stress than those who worked undisturbed.
What makes digital interruptions especially costly is their unpredictability. A colleague stopping by your desk follows social rules: you can ask them to come back later. A notification, by contrast, is engineered to be irresistible. Every ping carries the promise of something new—a like, a message, a headline—and the brain's reward system responds before rational judgement can intervene. Over time, this conditioning trains people to prefer shallow busyness over deep work, even when the shallow work produces nothing of value.
Some companies have begun to fight back with what they call "attention-friendly" policies: no-meeting mornings, email-free days, and default settings that silence non-urgent notifications. Early results are encouraging, with employees reporting both higher output and lower anxiety. The lesson for individuals is similar: protect a few hours of uninterrupted time each day as carefully as you protect a meeting with your boss. Depth, it turns out, is a skill that must be defended rather than assumed.
reading.questions:
1. What does the passage say is the real cost of frequent interruptions?
A) The seconds spent reading each message.
B) The time needed to rebuild concentration.
C) The stress of replying to colleagues.
D) The fear of missing important news.

2. Why are digital interruptions more costly than a colleague's visit?
A) They arrive in much larger numbers.
B) They are always about urgent matters.
C) They are designed to be irresistible.
D) They break social rules openly.

3. What does the conditioning of notifications train people to prefer?
A) Deep reading over quick replies.
B) Shallow busyness over deep work.
C) Silence over constant contact.
D) Rewards over rational judgement.

4. What are "attention-friendly" policies mentioned in the passage?
A) Banning all office email.
B) Forbidding colleagues to talk.
C) Creating protected uninterrupted time.
D) Paying employees to focus.

5. What is the passage's suggestion for individuals?
A) Defend daily hours of deep work.
B) Check email only twice a day.
C) Turn off all notifications forever.
D) Assume depth comes naturally.
reading.analysis:
1. B。第一段指出真正代价不是打断本身,而是大脑重建思路所需的时间(the time the brain needs to rebuild the original train of thought)。
2. C。第二段对比:同事造访受社交规则约束,而通知被刻意设计得难以抵抗(engineered to be irresistible)。
3. B。第二段末句:这种条件反射训练人们偏好 shallow busyness over deep work。
4. C。第三段列举 no-meeting mornings、email-free days 等,本质是创造受保护的不受打扰时间。A 过于绝对(仅 email-free days,非全面禁止)。
5. A。末句 Depth is a skill that must be defended rather than assumed,与建议个人像保护会议一样保护每天几小时深度时间一致。

translation.prompt:
请将以下中文段落翻译成英文:

过去几十年,中国在减贫方面取得了举世瞩目的成就。数以亿计的农村贫困人口摆脱了贫困,基础设施得到显著改善,教育、医疗等公共服务覆盖面大幅扩大。政府通过产业扶持、易地搬迁、教育资助等多种措施,帮助贫困地区建立自我发展的能力。国际社会普遍认为,中国的减贫经验为其他国家提供了重要借鉴。
translation.reference: Over the past few decades, China has achieved remarkable success in poverty reduction, attracting worldwide attention. Hundreds of millions of rural residents have been lifted out of poverty, infrastructure has been markedly improved, and public services such as education and healthcare have been extended to far more people. Through industrial support, relocation programmes and education subsidies, the government has helped impoverished areas build the capacity for self-development. The international community widely regards China's poverty-reduction experience as an important reference for other countries.
translation.notes: 要点:①「举世瞩目」译为 attracting worldwide attention,避免逐字硬译;②「数以亿计」用 hundreds of millions of;③「易地搬迁」即 relocation programmes;④「自我发展的能力」转译为 the capacity for self-development,更符合英文抽象名词偏好;⑤ 句式上用被动语态衔接分句,减少 and 堆叠。
